extracted.intended_audience: psychological scientists, humor researchers, and students of moral/emotional psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and experimental criteria for when events are perceived as humorous: a situation elicits humor when it is appraised as a violation, appraised as benign, and both appraisals occur simultaneously. The paper operationalizes these conditions, describes three routes to benign appraisal, and gives experimental measures and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation core conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation must be appraised as a violation, a situation must be appraised as benign, and these two appraisals must occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors propose these three jointly necessary and sufficient conditions as the central criterion for eliciting humor. If any one of the three is missing (no violation, not benign, or not simultaneous), humor is unlikely. This is the principal evaluative rule used across the studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation (perceived normative or threat breach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is often evoked by violations, including apparent threats, breaches of norms, or taboo content—anything that disrupts people’s sense of how the world ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations can be physical threats (play fighting, tickling), breaches of personal dignity (slapstick, physical deformities), linguistic norms (accents, malapropisms), social norms (eating from a sterile bedpan), or moral norms (bestiality, disrespect). The paper uses violation as the necessary 'threat' component of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness via alternative norm (conflicting norm interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation can seem benign if a salient norm suggests the behavior is wrong but another salient norm suggests it is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the chicken-sex scenario can be judged acceptable by a harm-based norm (no one is harmed). The paper’s Studies 2 and 3 show that when people can interpret a behavior as both wrong and not wrong (i.e., conflicting norm interpretations), they are more likely to be amused. Use alternative-norm framing to increase benign appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness via weak commitment to the violated norm
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation may seem benign if the observer is only weakly committed to the violated norm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 4 shows nonchurchgoers (low commitment to sanctity norm) were more amused than churchgoers at a church giving away a Hummer. To evaluate likely amusement, consider target/audience commitment strength to the relevant norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignness via psychological distance
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation can seem benign if it is psychologically distant — temporal, social, spatial, likelihood, or hypotheticality distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 5 used distance priming (far vs. near) and found distant violations elicited more amusement and more mixed amusement+disgust. Practical ways to increase benignness include emphasizing hypotheticality, temporal remove, or social distance. Comedian heuristics cited: 'Comedy is tragedy plus time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity / bisociation (holding two contradictory appraisals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires that two contradictory ideas about the same situation be held simultaneously (simultaneity, bisociation, incongruity+benign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Puns are a clear example: two meanings brought together. Study 2 directly measured whether participants could interpret a scenario as both 'wrong' and 'not wrong' and found simultaneity mediated displays of amusement. Simultaneity is the integrative mechanism connecting violation and benign appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-emotion expectation (amusement can co-occur with negative emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benign violations often elicit mixed emotions—amusement and negative emotions such as disgust—rather than purely positive affect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to views of humor as strictly positive, the authors predict and show empirically that benign moral violations produce laughter alongside disgust. Measurement approaches for mixed emotions (dichotomous yes/no for each emotion) are recommended and used in Studies 3–5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral and self-report indicators of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be measured via behavioral displays (smile, laugh observed) and self-reported amusement (did this scenario make you laugh?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The studies used both observer-coded smiles/laughter and simple yes/no self-report items. For mixed-emotion research, dichotomous measures of being 'amused' and 'disgusted' are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: malign or too-real violations are not funny
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations that are not perceived as benign (malign violations) — e.g., those that cause harm or seem too real/serious — tend to elicit strictly negative emotions and are less likely to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 3: the kitten scenario where the kitten is harmed is judged less benign and less amusing. The paper notes tragedies or genuinely harmful events are often incongruous but not humorous because they lack benign appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical levers to increase benign appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a violation more likely to be perceived as benign (and thus funnier): highlight an alternative acceptable norm, reduce perceived commitment to the violated norm, or increase psychological distance (temporal, social, hypotheticality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and heuristics: emphasize hypotheticality/exaggeration, remind viewers of an alternative norm (e.g., harm absent), use temporal distance or social distance. Comedic rules of thumb cited: temporal distance ('tragedy plus time'), social distance (making the victim distant/exaggerated) and exaggeration/hypotheticality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns and language violations as benign violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns are benign violations because they violate a language convention but are technically correct according to an alternative interpretation of a word or phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats linguistic violations as a category of violation that becomes humorous when an alternative, technically-correct interpretation renders the violation benign (Veatch, 1998). This provides a concrete subtype of benign violation useful for evaluating wordplay.
